title: Nvidia credit risk gauge hits new peak as SoftBank readies record bond issue

Investing.com - SoftBank Group is preparing to issue approximately 1 trillion yen ($6.26 billion) in seven-year corporate bonds targeting Japanese retail investors, a sale that would be the largest of its kind ever by a Japanese company.

The offering lands at a fraught moment for AI-linked credit globally, with Nvidia's 5-year credit default swap spread surpassing its late-July peak and long-term government yields reaching their highest levels in decades.

SoftBank is the most visible Asian proxy for the AI financing wave, having already raised a 1.6 billion yen hybrid bond in May 2026. The scale of the planned retail deal — set against record-high sovereign yields — makes it a direct test of whether retail demand in Japan can absorb AI infrastructure debt as institutional credit markets grow more selective.

Long-term borrowing costs from the U.S. to Germany and Japan hit their highest levels in decades, with investors pointing squarely at hyperscaler bond supply as a contributing force.

AI infrastructure debt now accounts for as much as 30% of net new issuance in some investment-grade indexes this year, according to private credit market commentary cited by Reuters.

Longer-duration corporate yields moved above 6% in July, raising all-in income from high-quality corporate credit but also driving greater investor selectivity given elevated issuance and tight starting valuations.

Japan's broader retail-targeted corporate bond market is on pace to hit a record 2.8 trillion yen this year, per Nikkei, suggesting demand has not dried up, but SoftBank's offering would dwarf anything attempted before.

Nvidia illustrates the credit stress building across the AI complex. Its 5-year CDS bid spread climbed to 80.77 basis points as of August 19, surpassing its late-July peak. That spread has risen roughly 90% year-to-date and more than doubled since late May.

Some of the widening reflects the simple mechanics of a larger debt stock to hedge rather than an imminent default scenario and Alphabet's recent bond sale in Australia still drew strong investor demand.

However, the directional signal is hard to ignore ahead of Nvidia's earnings report scheduled for next Wednesday, the first major test of its $500 billion AI financing narrative under capital-market scrutiny.

Nvidia has said it may back no more than 25% of the total itself, meaning the bulk of that capital must be raised externally into a market where yield competition from sovereigns is intensifying.

Oracle offers the starkest credit warning in the sector. Its 5-year CDS spread surpassed 200 basis points in July 2026, approximately four times the investment-grade corporate index and a level not seen since the 2008 financial crisis.

Every day the Zacks Equity Research analysts discuss the latest news and events impacting stocks and the financial markets. Stocks recently featured in the blog include: Oracle Corp. ORCL, Microsoft MSFT, Amazon AMZN and Alphabet GOOGL.

Here are highlights from Tuesday's Analyst Blog:

Should You Buy Oracle Stock Despite Its Big AI Datacenter Bet?

Oracle Corp. has turned itself into one of the most talked-about names in enterprise technology, largely because of the scale of its bet on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company is spending tens of billions of dollars building out AI data centers, funded partly through debt and equity issuance, and that capital intensity has made some investors nervous about the near-term path of free cash flow.

Yet a closer look at Oracle's underlying business, its rapidly expanding AI partnerships and its own forward-looking guidance suggests the near-term setup still favors buyers who can stomach the balance-sheet risk tied to this build-out, rather than investors waiting for full clarity before committing capital.

Shares of Oracle have lost 8.9% in the past six-month period, underperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's appreciation of 21.7%, a gap that reflects investor caution around Oracle's debt-funded capital spending rather than any slowdown in its underlying AI business.

AI-Driven Cloud Backlog Underpins the Growth Case

The clearest fundamental signal comes from Oracle's Remaining Performance Obligations, which reached $638 billion at the end of the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, up 363% year over year and $85 billion sequentially. Most of that increase reflects large-scale AI contracts, and importantly, the prepaid and customer-supplied hardware portions of these agreements now total $75 billion, which meaningfully reduces the amount of capital Oracle itself must raise to build its AI data centers going forward. 

Cloud infrastructure revenues surged 93% in the quarter to $5.8 billion, while the Oracle Multicloud AI Database grew 404%, making it the company's fastest-growing business ever. These figures point to underlying demand that is outrunning Oracle's aggressive capacity additions, a dynamic that should keep utilization and eventually margins moving in the right direction as newly built megawatts of data center capacity come online through fiscal 2027.

Salesforce is currently trading at a lower valuation multiple compared to historical averages, prompting investor debate over its intrinsic value.

Salesforce (CRM) generates free cash equal to 8.8% of its market value each year, while the median S&P 500 company manages just 4.3%. Yet over the last twelve months, as the index climbed 21%, Salesforce stock fell 17.5%. The market is making a very specific offer on this application software business, which currently trades around $190.97 a share. The question for investors is whether this is a genuine bargain on a cash machine, or a fair warning about what comes next.

Is This 8.8% Yield Built On A Durable Machine?

The cash flow is not a one-time event. It is the output of a $42.83 billion revenue business with durable profitability. Salesforce's operating margin over the last twelve months was 22%, comfortably above its 3-year average of 20%. This financial strength is rooted in its position as what management calls the "number 1 agentic CRM," selling software that automates sales, service, and marketing functions for its customers.

The company is leaning heavily into artificial intelligence to drive the next phase of growth. Its Agentforce products now represent an annual recurring revenue stream greater than $1 billion. Usage metrics are expanding rapidly; the company reported it processed 28.6 trillion tokens in its latest quarter, up 152% from the quarter prior. This is the engine: selling more AI-infused, high-margin software to a large existing customer base.

The Market Sees Lagging Bookings And A Drag From Older Clouds

For the stock's markdown to be correct, the market must believe this cash stream is set to shrink or stall. The concern, visible in the latest earnings call, is that the impressive AI adoption is not yet translating into broad-based financial strength. The investor debate centers on whether the new AI products can overcome softness in other parts of the business, such as its Tableau and Commerce Cloud offerings.

Skeptics point out that key leading indicators, like contract bookings, have not meaningfully outperformed guidance for the last 2 quarters. This raises a fair question about timing. A recent analysis asked if CRM stock passed the value-trap test, which is precisely the issue the market is weighing: are the strong AI signals enough to re-accelerate the entire company? For investors who prefer to own the entire software theme rather than a single name, a software ETF like IGV offers broader exposure.

Adobe's stock has declined to a historical support zone that has previously preceded upward price momentum. Trading around $254, it sits at a price level that has attracted increased buying volume in the past.

Adobe (ADBE), the company whose software powers much of the digital world, finds its stock back on familiar, contested ground. Trading around $254.04 a share, it sits at the lower boundary of a broader $250 to $280 historical price region that has attracted significant buying volume during previous market cycles. History is clear: when the stock has fallen to this level, buyers have consistently shown up. With the company executing a fundamental shift in strategy, the critical variable is whether this historical price level will continue to attract institutional and retail support.

The echoes of past standoffs are strong. The five previous defenses of this level produced an average peak gain of 63%. Some were quick skirmishes, like a 15-day rally in April 2019 that yielded a 6.3% gain. Others were the start of major campaigns, such as the defense in October 2019 that preceded a 158% surge, or the one in September 2022 that led to a 129% climb. The table of prior bounces shows a clear pattern of buyers seeing value here.

The business arrives at this floor profitable, but in a profound state of change.

A floor holds or breaks based on the health of the business that lands on it. Adobe arrives with solid vital signs: revenue over the last twelve months grew 11.5%, and its operating margin over the last twelve months is a healthy 36%. But the real story is a deliberate, company-altering pivot. Management is aggressively shifting to a "freemium" model to capture a new generation of users with AI-powered tools like Firefly and Express.

The goal is to build a large user funnel first and monetize it later. Early results show the funnel is filling. Management reports that its Creative Freemium monthly active users, or MAU, have grown from 50 million to 90 million year over year, while Acrobat and Express MAU increased from over 700 million to more than 850 million. This is a conscious trade: sacrifice immediate sales for a much larger audience.

The company's backlog has quietly swelled to a record size. Remaining performance obligations finished at $638 billion, a figure that redefines its growth trajectory. This massive book of business, up 363%, was bolstered by signing $67 billion in AI infrastructure contracts in a single quarter.

This operational reality stands in stark contrast to a stock trading at a discount to its own history. The market has not yet priced in this monumental shift in future revenue visibility. A rerate is the primary lever for upside if investors begin to value this backlog.

That's the story for Oracle (ORCL). The question is whether it's strong enough to deliver real upside from here, or whether today's price has already absorbed most of the optimism. Mostly yes. A modeled 3-year scenario projects a potential 62% increase for ORCL, and the operational story carries it. Compounding earnings are doing the heavy lifting, supplemented by a partial multiple re-rating. Here is the operational picture the math sits on top of:

The Math Behind A Re-Rating

The setup is unusual: revenue compounds and margins hold, but the multiple has compressed below where the business has historically traded. The math centers on that gap closing.

The P/E re-rates partially from today's 24.7x toward the 3-year average of 36.1x, landing at 27.6x. Revenue compounds at 14.7% and margins hold near 24%, taking earnings from $17.1B to roughly $24.7B. Fundamental earnings growth, supplemented by a modest multiple re-rating, is driving the majority of the price upside. Apply the higher multiple to the higher earnings and the stock lands near $237.33, roughly 62% above today.

Did the same lever drive ORCL's recent move, or was it something different? See the lever breakdown.

What Could Trigger The Re-Rating

The narrative could reset as this backlog converts to revenue. Management has already guided for an acceleration, with expected growth in total revenues of +34% for fiscal year 2027. This figure provides a concrete timeline for when the market must acknowledge the new growth profile.

What Could Validate The Discount

This rapid infrastructure buildout comes at a cost to profitability. Management explicitly stated the fiscal year 2027 gross margin will step down. This is a direct result of the timing for ramping up massive data center projects before they reach full revenue contribution.

Loading up on growth stocks while they're down big can set up investors for significant gains later on. It's important, however, to understand why they are struggling before buying them, so that investors are aware of any risks involving them.

Three growth stocks that may look incredibly appealing to long-term investors right now are Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU), and Coupang (NYSE:CPNG). Here's why they may be worth buying, while they're down more than 50% from their highs.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Oracle

Database giant Oracle has come under pressure this year due to its rising debt load and exposure to OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Since the start of the year, Oracle's shares have fallen by 26%. On Monday, it closed below $147 -- a significant pullback from the 52-week high of $345.72 it reached last year.

In its most recent earnings report, the company said it still expects to raise roughly $40 billion for the current fiscal year through a combination of debt and equity. While the business has been growing at a fast pace and expects revenue to rise between 27% and 29% during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, which runs through the end of August, investors appear more concerned about the long-term risks it faces.

There is undoubtedly risk here with Oracle, but that's arguably priced into its valuation; the stock is trading at 18 times its estimated future earnings (based on analyst expectations). That's a fairly low multiple for a top tech stock such as Oracle. For investors willing to take on the risk, there could be some attractive upside ahead if the company can calm investor fears.

Intuit

Shares of software company Intuit have nosedived nearly 50% since the start of 2026. Investor fears about artificial intelligence (AI) and the possibility that it could disrupt software businesses led to many quality stocks, including Intuit, falling sharply in the early part of the year.

While Intuit has begun to rally in recent months, it still has a long way to go before it fully recovers from the sharp sell-off. Yesterday, it closed at around $335, which is more than 50% below its 52-week high of $719.10.

Intuit's business still looks to be in solid shape, with the company reporting revenue growth of 10% in its third-quarter results, which went up until the end of April. I believe the market has overreacted in the case of Intuit, as its tax and accounting software isn't something AI could easily replace, nor is it something consumers and businesses would easily trust even if it did.
